title: Knowledge Graph-based Vienna District Similarity and Lifestyle Recommendation
name: Moritz Lindner

LO1.text: I trained TransE and RotatE on the materialised KG (five seeds each), evaluated link prediction, similarity stability and a completion experiment, and use the embeddings for district similarity in the service.

LO2.text: Six Nemo programs (103 rules) with a recursive taxonomy, recursive transit reachability, aggregation, stratified negation and existential object creation for explained recommendations; verified against independent implementations and explained with derivation traces.

LO3.text: Not included, as planned in the one-pager.

LO4.text: Relations (Datalog facts) as main model, triples for the embeddings and an RDF export with named graphs for ground and derived facts; compared with property graphs, SPARQL and a plain feature table.

LO5.text: Layered architecture with offline materialisation and per-request reasoning, designed along the responsibility of knowing/doing between KG and application.

LO6.text: Discussed the cost of the transit recursion, materialisation versus per-request reasoning, reasoner limitations and the transductive limits of the embeddings.

LO7.text: Built the KG from four open sources with loaders and schema-mapping rules, including district resolution by coordinates and record linkage.

LO8.text: Completed the KG with rules (1.9 M derived facts) and with the embedding (completion experiment, suggested facts), and cleaned it by record linkage and conflict detection.

LO9.text: District recommendation for newcomers to Vienna based on integrated open data.

LO10.text: Related the location KG to location scoring in banking and insurance.

LO11.text: Web application with a JSON API: preference-based, explained recommendations with commute constraints, similar districts and district profiles with provenance.

LO12.text: Rule-derived facts train the embeddings and learned similarity flows back into the rules; discussed where each side is stronger.

ai_project.text: Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant: it implemented most of the code (data loaders, Nemo rules, embedding pipeline, web application, tests) according to my decisions on scope, data sources, preference categories, architecture and user interface, which I reviewed and tested.
